newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Investment, demand to boost Hungary GDP - thinktank.
newsitem.headline: Investment, demand to boost Hungary GDP - thinktank.

text.p: Hungary's economy would return to growth this year, expanding by 2.5 percent, on the back of rising investment and domestic demand, GKI Economic Research said on Wednesday.

However, growth is likely to result in a rise in current account deficit and therefore the government should prevent an unjustified increase of household consumption in 1997, GKI, a state-owned but independent think tank, said.
It said last year's substantial reduction in the deficits in the current and budget accounts created the foundations for growth.
"GKI assumes that the deficits will widen slightly in line with economic growth," GKI Managing Director Andras Vertes told a news conference.

"If imports increase quickly in the interest of investments and modernisation, that's good," he said. "But a substantial rise in consumption would be unfavourable and jeopardise the results of economic stabilisation."

GKI said household consumption would grow by one to two percent this year -- still a reasonably safe expansion -- after an estimated three percent drop in 1996, and compared to the official target of up to 0.5 percent.
Net wages are likely to increase by 22 to 23 percent, with real wages growing up to three percent after latest tax changes compared with a five percent fall last year, GKI added.

GKI said investment, which dropped by an estimated three percent in 1996, would grow by 10 percent this year, boosted by the increasing activity in state-funded infrastructure projects and growing business at commercial firms trying to boost their exports.

Exports are likely to increase by 10 percent, compared with 13 percent last year, while imports would rise by 11 percent after 12 percent in 1996, boosting the foreign trade deficit by $400 to $500 million, to $3-3.2 billion, GKI said.
However, the government should not allow the deficit to widen by more than that, and larger imports should serve the modernisation of the economy, according to GKI.
Vertes said Hungarian companies needed investment to improve their competitiveness, which will be weakened by the trade and monetary policy measures planned for this year.
Hungary plans to phase out its four percent import surcharge by July, increasing competition on the domestic market with imported products.
The monthly devaluation rate will be reduced to 1.1 percent on April 1 from 1.2 percent, and the government said it may further cut the rate in July.
However, a cut is not likely until September or October, and the reduction will not be larger than 10 basis points, Vertes said.
